title.narrative: Tbilisi and Batumi Shelter Cities alongside the Telavi Art Residence: Strengthening HRDs' resilience amid global crises and the impacts of aggressive war

description.narrative: HRDs, civil activists, journalists, and cultural workers from Belarus, Ukraine, Russia, Central Asia and the North Caucasus are the primary beneficiaries of Tbilisi Shelter City.

Tbilisi Shelter City is a project and organization aimed at providing temporary relocation and rehabilitation for human rights defenders (HRDs) at risk. The program provides for relocation for 3 months to a safe zone in Georgia, as well as creating an enabling environment for professional development, physical and psychological recovery of HRDs. Additionally, the program is designed to reduce risks and help HRDs temporarily leave a dangerous situation. While participating in the program, HRDs are provided with accommodation in safe conditions, educational and skills development opportunities, and the opportunity to make new professional contacts. They also receive psychological and medical assistance, if needed. During the program, participants received rehabilitation services, underwent costly laboratory and instrumental tests, as well as numerous consultations with doctors of various specialties. This allowed for the identification of serious health conditions and the diagnosis of various diseases. Based on the examination results, appropriate treatment was prescribed and administered, which continues after the participants return to their home countries. It shows a specific set of actions for each participant that leads to progress and improvement in their condition. TSC implements two resettlement programs: Short-term relocation/regular enrollment (up to 3 months, in low and medium threat cases) to strengthen the capacity of HRDs and prevent occupational burnout; Emergency relocation (without defined timeline, in case of imminent danger in their home country). During the reporting period, the TSC conducted 5 regular enrollments. Participants of the regular enrollments received the following services: accommodation, medical assistance, scholarship (monthly), individual sessions with the psychologist, medical SPA and physiological treatments, networking events, thematic trainings. Case manager services are available to each participant. They include assistance in adapting to a new environment, serving as a social worker and a liaison between the HRD, the country and the program. A dedicated medical manager assists with medical issues, and works with external medical staff to develop an individualized rehabilitation/treatment plan that meets the beneficiaries' needs. HRDs took part in trainings in various areas such as psychological burnout prevention, working with secondary trauma, security training, fundraising training. The security trainings also included individual consultations with experts, where participants were able to develop individual security plans to address the most severe threats they may face. As a result of the fundraising training, beneficiaries received the opportunity for individual support/mini-grants from partner organizations (after contacting them). Moreover, beneficiaries were taught English, pottery, and social theatre. Pottery helps reduce burnout and stress and express their emotions through art and working with clay. An important activity of the program is social theatre, through which participants develop social skills and intercultural interaction through role-playing.
The project objectives were the following: ● Relocate HRDs from the unsafe environment ● Provide psychological and physical rehabilitation ● Provide HRD with new skills and strengthen his/her network

activity-date.narrative: The project was actually executed and completed ahead of schedule on October 20, 2024.

organisation.narrative: Center for Participation and Development (CPD) works with youth and minorities promoting civil integration and participation of vulnerable groups in decision-making processes, as well as the development of a tolerant society in Georgia and in the Eastern Partnership region by raising the level of civic consciousness, harnessing advocacy skills among vulnerable groups, working on formal and non-formal education. Another important direction of the work of CDP is the protection of human rights defenders.

department.narrative: The highest body of CPD is the Board, which is elected for a term of 4 years. Chairman of the board - Agit Mirzoev. Board members - Giorgi Sordia, Arnold Stepanian, Tea Bulia Executive Director - Giorgi Marjanishvili.

recipient-country.narrative: Georgia is well known as a rehab country for many HRDs who were threatened, tortured, or suffering from psychological health problems. Moreover, Georgia can offer a more comfortable environment for HRDs from the region due to common cultural background and history. HRDs do not have to be accustomed to the new cultural environment when relocating here. Citizens of Central Asian states, Belarus, Russia, and other post-soviet countries do not need visas to enter Georgia, which increases the speed of relocation and makes possible emergency transfers arranged within hours. This makes the shelter in Georgia much better accessible for HRDs from the region in comparison to shelters located in the EU.

sector.narrative: Tbilisi Shelter City is a project founded by the Center for Participation and Development aimed to provide temporary relocation (planned and emergency) and rehabilitation for human rights defenders at risk.
